items.prose: Two threads both call `work()`, which uses these five names.
items.question: Which are shared by both threads? Select all that apply.

options.text: The heap block behind the global `cache`

options.why: `thread_local` gives each thread its own copy.
Each call of `work` has its own `i` on its own stack.
A plain local lives on the calling thread's stack.

feedback.correct: `visits` and the block that `cache` points to.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which exist once, or are reached through a reference?

byKey.i: A loop counter is a local, so each thread has its own.
byKey.buf: Each call gets its own `buf` on its own stack.

explain.text: A `static` local exists once per process, and every thread can follow a global pointer to the heap. Plain locals such as `i` and `buf` live on each thread's own stack. `thread_local` gives each thread its own `depth`.

items.prose: Creating a thread costs 15 µs. A handler makes a new thread for every message, at 100,000 messages a second.
items.question: How many cores does creating the threads use?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the cost by the rate.

byKey.fifteen: You slipped a power of ten: $15 \times 10^{-6} \times 10^5 = 1.5$.
byKey.tenth: You slipped a power of ten the other way.

explain.text: $15 \times 10^{-6}$ s $\times 100{,}000 = 1.5$ s of work every second. That is one and a half cores spent only on starting threads. A pool of threads made once avoids it.

items.prose: `x` is a `std::atomic<int>` at 0. Thread A loads it, adds 1 and stores it back, in three steps. Thread B calls `x.fetch_add(1)` twice.
items.question: How many of the 10 interleavings end with `x` at 3?

widget.accept: 3: both of B's adds fall outside A's load-to-store gap.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which of B's adds survive A's store?

byKey.two: You counted only the two serial orders. B can also add once before A loads and once after A stores.
byKey.four: 4 is the count that ends at 2, with one of B's adds lost.

explain.text: A's store writes what A loaded plus 1, wiping any add made in between. `x` ends at 3 only when neither of B's adds falls between A's load and store. That leaves both adds before A, one either side, or both after: 3 of 10.

items.prose: Three lanes each run load `x`, add, store `x`, from `x = 0`. Lane A adds 1, lane B adds 2 and lane C adds 4.
items.question: Which finals can happen? Select all that apply.

options.why: Every store writes a load plus at least 1.
The three adds total 7, so no store can write more.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which adds can the last store carry?

explain.text: The last store writes its load plus its own add. Its load may have seen any mix of the other adds, so 1 to 7 can all happen. Only the 6 orders that run each lane whole keep all three adds and reach 7.

items.prose: Threads P, Q and R take locks in the orders ABC, CD and DA. Each holds what it has while it takes the next.
items.question: Can they deadlock, and what is the fix?

options.text: Yes: A to B to C to D to A; reverse one thread
No: no two threads take the same pair of locks
options.why: A cycle can run through three threads and four locks; follow the edges.

options.text: Yes, and nothing short of one global lock fixes it
options.why: Reversing one thread's order breaks the cycle.

options.text: Only if two of them start at once
options.why: All three must each hold a lock at once, and that can happen.

feedback.correct: Yes. Reverse one thread: R taking A then D gives the order A, B, C, D.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Draw an edge for each thread.

explain.text: The edges A to B, B to C, C to D and D to A form a ring. If R takes A then D, every edge follows A, B, C, D.

items.prose: T1 takes lock A then B. T2 first reads `x`, then takes B then A. A lane cannot step while the lock it wants is held.
items.question: How many of the 14 legal schedules deadlock?

widget.accept: 3: T1's first lock can come before, between or after T2's first two steps.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. When does each lane hold its first lock?

byKey.two: 2 is the count without T2's read. The read gives T1's first lock three places.

explain.text: Both lanes stick when T1 holds A and T2 holds B, before either second lock. T1's one step can sit before, between or after T2's read and lock: 3 orders. The other 11 schedules finish.

items.prose: The load-buffering test. Thread A reads `x` into `r1`, then sets `y = 1`. Thread B reads `y` into `r2`, then sets `x = 1`. Both start at 0. Suppose the four steps run one at a time, in some order.
items.question: Which pairs (r1, r2) can occur? Select all that apply.

options.why: Each lane loads before it stores, so the first load always reads 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Can both loads see the other lane's store?

byKey.p11: The first step of any order is a load, and it reads 0.

explain.text: The first step of any order is a load, so at least one register is 0. That rules out (1, 1) and leaves the other three. With `relaxed` atomics, C++ still allows (1, 1): each lane's two accesses touch different variables.

items.prose: A consumer checks whether the queue is empty, then waits for a notify. A producer pushes, then notifies. Sometimes the consumer sleeps forever with an item queued.
items.question: Why?

options.text: The notify fell in the gap between check and wait
A spurious wakeup confused the condition variable
options.why: A spurious wakeup ends a wait early; it never makes one endless.

options.text: The queue was full, so the consumer was stuck
options.why: A full queue blocks the producer, not the consumer.
There is only one consumer, so either wakes it, if it is waiting.

feedback.correct: The notify fell between the check and the wait.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. When does a notify wake nobody?

explain.text: A notify wakes only threads already waiting. If the push and notify land after the check but before the wait, the consumer sleeps through them. Holding the mutex across the check and the wait closes that gap.

items.prose: Two counters sit on one 64-byte cache line. Each thread adds to its own counter 10 million times. An add costs 60 ns when the line moves between cores. It costs 1 ns when the line stays in one core's L1.
items.question: Moving one counter to its own line saves each thread how many ms?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the new cost from the old cost, then multiply.

byKey.full: 600 ms is the time before. The add still costs 1 ns afterwards.
byKey.after: 10 ms is the time after. The question asks what is saved.

explain.text: The threads never share a counter, but they share a line, so the line moves on every add. This is false sharing. Each add falls from 60 ns to 1 ns, so $10^7 \times 59$ ns is 590 ms saved.
